analysis.one_liner: Ended the federal tax deduction for oil and chemical spill cleanup costs when the polluter's cleanup fails federal standards.
analysis.headline: Passed months after the Exxon Valdez spill, the bill won a Finance Committee hearing but died there, and companies kept deducting oil spill cleanup costs from their taxes.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Exxon Valdez disaster, this bill would have changed the tax code so that companies causing oil or hazardous substance spills could no longer deduct their cleanup costs from their taxes unless they actually did the cleanup properly under federal standards. The money the government would otherwise have effectively refunded to polluters would flow instead into federal oil-spill cleanup and Superfund accounts. The bill never received a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee after one hearing and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently subsidize polluters' cleanups through the tax deduction — the bill's own findings noted the Coast Guard recovered only $72 million of the $144 million the public spent on cleanups between 1972 and 1987. It would also benefit coastal communities, waterways, and fisheries by giving polluters a strong financial reason to clean up thoroughly, and it would shore up federal cleanup funds by routing the recovered revenue to the Clean Water Act fund and Superfund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities hit by spills

how_it_helps.text: It denied a federal tax deduction for oil and hazardous substance cleanup costs — including legal expenses and restitution payments — unless the polluter earned certification that it made a good faith effort to meet federal cleanup law, or the spill was caused by an act of God, war, government negligence, or a third party.
It barred companies from recouping the lost deduction through net operating loss write-offs, closing a route to recover the money anyway.
It directed the added revenue to the Clean Water Act revolving fund for oil removal and the Superfund for hazardous substances, and required annual Treasury reporting on cleanup spending.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and chemical companies whose cleanups fall short of federal standards: they would lose the deduction for cleanup costs, legal fees, and restitution payments, and could not recover it through net operating loss write-offs. Responsible companies that clean up properly keep their deduction.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies that spill and clean up poorly

drawbacks.text: The certification process gives the EPA Administrator or Coast Guard Commandant discretion over whether a company keeps its deduction, which could invite dispute and delay over what counts as a 'good faith effort' at cleanup.

Denying the deduction and blocking net-operating-loss offsets raises the effective cost of even partial cleanup compliance, and companies facing a catastrophic spill might argue the penalty-like tax treatment pushes marginal operators toward bankruptcy rather than cleanup.

The bill required Treasury to estimate the revenue given away from 1970 to 1988, but set no revenue target of its own and relied on appropriations for the fund transfers, so the money could sit unappropriated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — taxpayers should not effectively subsidize cleanup costs when the polluter's cleanup fails federal standards — is sound and narrow, aimed squarely at a gap in existing law. The cost side is real but modest: legitimate full-cleanups would still be deductible, and the main burden falls on companies whose cleanup falls short. The bill was lightly developed (it never moved beyond a hearing) and made no attempt to estimate its revenue impact itself beyond ordering a Treasury study. The bigger cost was opportunity: the comprehensive oil-spill liability regime enacted later in 1990 (OPA 90) became the operative law instead.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, got one hearing in June 1989, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Harry Reid introduced the bill on April 13, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
The committee held a single hearing on June 21, 1989 (printed as S.Hrg. 101-572), but never reported the bill or voted on it.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died in committee with no further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies and other polluters kept deducting cleanup costs from their federal taxes; taxpayers continued absorbing part of the cost of inadequate cleanups.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluting companies, which kept the tax break

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end tax deductions for polluters' cleanup costs and pushed for a hearing in the Finance Committee.

for.name: 15 of 100 Senate cosponsors (11 Democrats, 4 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties.

against.name: Oil and petroleum shipping industry
against.what_they_did: The bill would have stripped a tax deduction the industry's members routinely claimed for spill cleanup costs; the bill died in committee without a floor vote.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after a single June 1989 hearing, never reporting the bill to the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were senators — 11 Democrats and 4 Republicans — so the bill had support from both parties, though it never reached a vote where a party split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill stripped a tax deduction for spill cleanup costs whenever the cleanup failed federal standards, and blocked offsetting the loss through net operating losses — raising the price of a bad cleanup.
Hazardous substance cleanup costs would lose deductibility under the same conditions, routing the added revenue to the Superfund.

The bill's own findings noted the Coast Guard recovered only $72 million of the $144 million the public spent on cleanups from 1972 to 1987, and that deductible cleanup costs amount to ordinary taxpayers subsidizing polluters.
